questions.stem: To keep the room quieter while you work, you pull the Pro Tools master fader down 8 dB and leave it there. You then bounce the mix. What do you predict?
options: The bounced mix file is changed, coming out about 8 dB lower
The bounced mix file is unchanged, since the master only sets room level
The bounced mix file is unchanged, since bounces are always written at unity
The bounced mix file is changed, but only in its low frequency balance
key: The bounced mix file is changed, coming out about 8 dB lower
questions.page: Calibration: Speaker and Headphone Level Calibration
questions.quote: Using it as a volume control changes your final mix file, sometimes for the worse.
questions.why: Predict the consequence of using the master fader as a listening volume control.

questions.stem: Your active monitors connect to an audio interface that has an output knob. You have no monitor controller. Which control should be your main overall listening volume?
options: The output volume control on the interface
The master fader in your Pro Tools session
The level knobs on the back of each monitor
A gain plug-in on the master track
key: The output volume control on the interface
questions.page: Calibration: Speaker and Headphone Level Calibration
questions.quote: This is sometimes a knob on the front of the interface, and it is sometimes controlled digitally through software. It functions like a small monitor section, similar to what you would find on an analog console.
questions.why: Choose the correct overall volume control in a setup with no monitor controller.

questions.stem: You mix on headphones plugged straight into your laptop headphone jack, with no interface. Which control should set your overall listening level?
options: The system volume control of the computer
The master fader in your Pro Tools session
A trim plug-in on the master track
The channel faders on every track equally
key: The system volume control of the computer
questions.page: Calibration: Speaker and Headphone Level Calibration
questions.quote: If you are listening on headphones plugged directly into the computer, this is likely the last gain stage before your ears.
questions.why: Choose a listening control that does not alter the mix file in a headphone-only setup.

questions.stem: During speaker calibration your left monitor, playing alone, reads 85 dB SPL at the mix position. What is the correct next step?
options: Play the right monitor alone and match it to the same meter reading
Play both monitors together and set the pair to read 85 dB SPL
Mark the controller position now, since one speaker sets the level
Adjust the right monitor with the pair playing until it sounds even
key: Play the right monitor alone and match it to the same meter reading
questions.page: Calibration: Speaker and Headphone Level Calibration
questions.quote: Test one speaker at a time. Confirm both speakers measure exactly the same before moving on.
questions.why: Carry out the one-speaker-at-a-time matching step correctly.

questions.stem: Your speakers are rated for 105 dB SPL, your calibration noise averages -20 dBFS, and you want 20 dB of headroom. What should the SPL meter read at the mix position when you finish?
options: 85 dB SPL
105 dB SPL
65 dB SPL
95 dB SPL
key: 85 dB SPL
questions.page: Calibration: Speaker and Headphone Level Calibration
questions.quote: if you want 20 dB of headroom, your test signal averages -20 dBFS, and your speakers are rated for 105 dB SPL or higher, aim for 85 dB SPL on your meter at the mix position.
questions.why: Work out the target SPL from headroom and test signal level.

questions.stem: A classmate calibrates the studio monitors by playing a favorite commercial song and reading the SPL meter. Why is this the weakest choice of test signal?
options: Loudness and frequency content vary widely from song to song
Songs are mastered too quietly to give a usable meter reading
Music has equal energy per frequency, which tilts the reading bright
Stereo music cannot be sent to one speaker at a time
key: Loudness and frequency content vary widely from song to song
questions.page: Calibration: Speaker and Headphone Level Calibration
questions.quote: Frequency content and overall loudness vary greatly between songs, which makes music the least reliable of the three test signals.
questions.why: Judge why music is an unreliable calibration signal.

questions.stem: You try to balance your monitors using white noise, and it sounds brighter and louder toward the top of the spectrum. What explains this?
options: Each higher octave holds more frequencies, so it carries more energy
White noise falls about 3 dB per octave, so the lows are masked
White noise is shaped to match how human ears hear loudness
White noise has equal energy per octave, which favors the highs
key: Each higher octave holds more frequencies, so it carries more energy
questions.quote: Since white noise has equal energy per frequency, an octave with twice as many frequencies in it ends up with twice as much total energy.
questions.why: Diagnose why white noise is a poor, bright calibration signal.

questions.stem: You play pink noise into an analyzer that displays the total energy in each octave band. What should the display show?
options: About the same level in every octave band
Level rising about 3 dB with each higher octave
Level falling about 6 dB with each higher octave
Level peaking in the midrange and falling at both ends
key: About the same level in every octave band
questions.quote: That means the low octaves and the high octaves each carry the same total power, which matches how we perceive loudness across the frequency range far better than white noise does.
questions.why: Predict how pink noise reads on an octave-band display.

questions.stem: Your monitors measure correctly with pink noise, yet level matching during real mixing sessions still feels inconsistent. Which test signal is designed to close that gap?
options: M Noise, built from music that keeps its loudness and crest factor
White noise, since equal energy per frequency is more neutral
Brown noise, since its steeper tilt resembles a finished mix
A 1 kHz reference tone, since one frequency is easier to read
key: M Noise, built from music that keeps its loudness and crest factor
questions.quote: M Noise is built from real musical program material that has been processed to retain the statistical loudness and crest-factor characteristics of actual music while remaining repeatable and measurable like a test tone.
questions.why: Choose a calibration signal that behaves like real program material.

questions.stem: You need the meters in two different studios to agree on what a given digital level reads. Which test signal fits this job?
options: A steady 1 kHz tone at a defined dBFS level
A sine sweep through the full audio range
Pink noise played at a comfortable level
A well mixed song that holds a steady level
key: A steady 1 kHz tone at a defined dBFS level
questions.quote: a steady single-frequency tone at a defined digital level, used to align meter calibration between different pieces of gear or different rooms, rather than to test frequency response.
questions.why: Choose the right signal for aligning meters between rooms.

questions.stem: A classmate presses a handheld SPL meter against a headphone earcup, reads 85 dB, and calls the headphones calibrated. Which reasons show why this reading is not valid? (Mark all that apply.)
options: The pad seal changes the pressure that reaches the ear
Headphone placement on the head changes the pressure
Your own pinna and ear canal shape the level at the eardrum
Headphone drivers are too quiet for a handheld meter to detect
The meter must be set to read dBFS instead of dB SPL
Pink noise cannot be played through headphones at 85 dB
key: The pad seal changes the pressure that reaches the ear
Headphone placement on the head changes the pressure
Your own pinna and ear canal shape the level at the eardrum
questions.page: Calibration: Speaker and Headphone Level Calibration
questions.quote: The pressure at your eardrum depends on the enclosed ear volume, pad seal, headphone placement, your pinna, and your ear canal, none of which a handheld meter accounts for.
questions.why: Diagnose why a handheld SPL meter cannot calibrate headphones.

questions.stem: Using the loudness-matching method this course teaches, which actions are part of setting your headphone reference level? (Mark all that apply.)
options: Calibrate the monitors first, before touching the headphones
Match the headphone loudness to the calibrated monitors by ear
Set the headphones to read 85 dB SPL on a handheld meter
Calibrate the headphones first, then match the monitors to them
Use a mixing level a friend finds comfortable on their headphones
key: Calibrate the monitors first, before touching the headphones
Match the headphone loudness to the calibrated monitors by ear
questions.page: Calibration: Speaker and Headphone Level Calibration
questions.quote: calibrate your monitors first, then match the headphones to that calibrated sound field by ear.
questions.why: Apply the order and method for a repeatable headphone reference.

questions.stem: During loudness matching, the headphones sound quieter than the calibrated monitors on the same pink noise. What do you change?
options: Only the headphone amplifier or headphone output level
The clip gain on the pink noise region in Pro Tools
The master fader, then recalibrate the monitors to match
The monitor controller, lowering it until the two match
key: Only the headphone amplifier or headphone output level
questions.page: Calibration: Speaker and Headphone Level Calibration
questions.quote: Adjust only the headphone amplifier or headphone output level until the headphones sound approximately equal in loudness to the calibrated monitors.
questions.why: Choose the one gain stage allowed to move while matching headphones.

questions.stem: A classmate says the headphone mixing target is 80 dBA because a guideline allows 80 dBA for up to 40 hours a week. What is wrong with that reasoning?
options: That figure is a hearing-safety exposure limit, not a mixing target
That figure is the loudspeaker target, so headphones need 85 dBA
That figure is correct, but only when read on a handheld meter
That figure is too low, since all mixing must be done at 85 dB SPL
key: That figure is a hearing-safety exposure limit, not a mixing target
questions.page: Calibration: Speaker and Headphone Level Calibration
questions.quote: That is a hearing-safety recommendation, not a mixing calibration target.
questions.why: Separate hearing-safety limits from calibration targets.

questions.stem: You mix on closed-back headphones. Which conditions will likely cost you low end at the ear and tempt you to add too much bass? (Mark all that apply.)
options: Wearing glasses under the earpads
Long hair caught under the earpads
Earpads that are badly worn
Earpads that seal fully around the ear
A fresh set of earpads fitted today
Headphones sitting evenly on the head
key: Wearing glasses under the earpads
Long hair caught under the earpads
Earpads that are badly worn
questions.page: Calibration: Speaker and Headphone Level Calibration
questions.quote: A broken seal loses the low end first. Glasses, long hair and a worn earpad all cost you bass you will then try to fix in the mix.
questions.why: Diagnose headphone seal problems that skew bass decisions.

questions.stem: You calibrated to 85 dB SPL, but that is far too loud for the quiet acoustic project you are mixing. How do you set a comfortable working level without losing your reference?
options: Play a similar reference song, lower the main controller, and mark that spot
Pull the master fader down until the mix feels comfortable to hear
Recalibrate the monitors with pink noise to a lower SPL for this project
Keep mixing at 85 dB SPL, since any other level breaks calibration
key: Play a similar reference song, lower the main controller, and mark that spot
questions.page: Calibration: Speaker and Headphone Level Calibration
questions.quote: Turn the main level down until it feels comfortable, then mark that new position so you know exactly what to return to.
questions.why: Set a practical working level while keeping a repeatable reference.

questions.stem: You are building the three-track MS decode in Pro Tools. Which settings belong on the MS R track? (Mark all that apply.)
options: Pan it hard right
Activate polarity invert on an EQ 3 1-Band insert
Carry only the Side signal on it
Pan it center with the Mid
Insert a short delay to offset the Side
Carry only the Mid signal on it
key: Pan it hard right
Activate polarity invert on an EQ 3 1-Band insert
Carry only the Side signal on it
questions.quote: The duplicate Side track. Pan hard right. Insert EQ 3 1-Band and activate the polarity invert button. This track carries the inverted Side signal only.
questions.why: Configure the inverted Side track of an MS decode.

questions.stem: A classmate decodes MS using a phase shift plug-in on MS R instead of a polarity invert. Why is polarity invert the right tool?
options: It flips the whole waveform at every frequency at the same time
It shifts only the low frequencies and leaves the highs alone
It delays the signal slightly, which widens the stereo image
It lowers the Side level by 6 dB, which balances the decode
key: It flips the whole waveform at every frequency at the same time
questions.quote: Polarity invert flips the entire waveform 180 degrees at all frequencies simultaneously. This is what MS decoding requires.
questions.why: Choose and justify polarity invert over phase shift.

questions.stem: You duplicate the Side track with Option + Shift + D, and the new track appears with no audio regions on it. What went wrong?
options: Playlist was not checked in the Duplicate Track dialog
Insert After Last Selected Track was left checked
The stereo track was split into mono before duplicating
The Side track was still in a group with the Mid track
key: Playlist was not checked in the Duplicate Track dialog
questions.quote: If Playlist is not checked in the Duplicate Track dialog, the new track will be empty.
questions.why: Diagnose an empty duplicate track in Pro Tools.

questions.stem: Your decoded MS orchestra recording sounds too wide against the rest of the mix. What is the right adjustment?
options: Lower both Side track faders together by the same amount
Lower the MS C fader so the Mid sits further back
Lower only the MS R fader until the image narrows
Raise both Side track faders together by the same amount
key: Lower both Side track faders together by the same amount
questions.quote: pull both Side tracks down together for a narrower image, push them up for a wider one. Keep them matched, or the image pulls to one side.
questions.why: Control MS width without pulling the image off center.

questions.stem: After building the MS matrix you solo MS C and hear a wide stereo spread. What does this tell you?
options: The routing is wrong, since MS C should give a stable center image
The routing is right, since MS C should carry the full stereo spread
The Side faders are too low, so the center has lost its focus
MS C also needs polarity invert to pull its image to center
key: The routing is wrong, since MS C should give a stable center image
questions.quote: Solo MS C and listen. You should hear a clear, stable center image with no stereo spread. If it sounds wide, the routing is incorrect.
questions.why: Verify an MS decode by listening to the Mid track.

questions.stem: A client asks why you recorded a location session in Mid-Side. Which are real advantages of MS? (Mark all that apply.)
options: The recording stays mono compatible
Stereo width can be adjusted after recording
The raw file plays back as normal stereo with no decoding
The Side mic removes room ambience from the recording
Width is locked in by the mic angle at the session
key: The recording stays mono compatible
Stereo width can be adjusted after recording
questions.quote: MS gives you mono-compatible recordings and lets you adjust the stereo width after recording by changing the level of the Side signal.
questions.why: Justify choosing MS for a recording.

questions.stem: You import 02_Pair_FrontMS and play it as an ordinary stereo track. The source sits hard left and the right side sounds diffuse and odd. Why?
options: The file holds raw Mid and Side signals that must be decoded first
The file was recorded out of polarity and needs flipping on the left
The pan law on the stereo track is set too low for playback
The left mic was a figure-8 aimed away from the source
key: The file holds raw Mid and Side signals that must be decoded first
questions.quote: These are raw signals. They cannot be listened to directly as a stereo pair without decoding them first.
questions.why: Diagnose an undecoded MS file on playback.

questions.stem: You are measuring monitor level at the listening position and the reading is 3 dB low. What is the disciplined way to proceed?
options: Make one controlled adjustment, then measure again before anything else
Raise the controller and interface output together, then measure
Raise the master fader 3 dB so the meter reads on target
Adjust by ear until it sounds right, then skip the second reading
key: Make one controlled adjustment, then measure again before anything else
questions.quote: Measure the playback level at the listening position, make one controlled adjustment, then measure again.
questions.why: Apply the measure, adjust, measure loop during calibration.

questions.stem: You play the calibration noise from a media player app, while your mixes play from Pro Tools through a different output. What is the problem?
options: The noise must run through the same output path you mix through
The noise must be played at 0 dBFS to give a valid reading
Media player apps cannot play back 24-bit reference files
Nothing, since any playback source gives the same level reading
key: The noise must run through the same output path you mix through
questions.quote: Open the supplied reference-noise file and route it through the same output path used for mixing.
questions.why: Diagnose a calibration done through the wrong signal path.
